title: Real numbers
subject: Mathematics
summary: Real numbers include every rational and irrational number, so they cover all points on the number line.
points: A rational number can be written as p/q; an irrational number cannot, such as √2 or π.
Every composite number has a unique prime factorisation (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic).
Rational numbers have terminating or repeating decimal expansions; irrational ones do not repeat.

formulas.name: HCF and LCM
formulas.expr: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

example: √2 is irrational because it cannot be written as a fraction of integers; 0.75 = 3/4 is rational.
mistakes: Thinking every square root is irrational; √9 = 3 is rational.

title: Polynomials
subject: Mathematics
summary: A polynomial is a sum of terms with non-negative integer powers of a variable; its degree is the highest power.
points: A zero of a polynomial is a value that makes it equal zero.
The Remainder Theorem says p(x) divided by (x − a) leaves remainder p(a).
The Factor Theorem says (x − a) is a factor exactly when p(a) = 0.
example: For x² − 5x + 6, the zeroes are 2 and 3, and 2 + 3 = 5 = −(−5)/1.
mistakes: Writing the sum of zeroes as b/a instead of −b/a.

title: Pair of linear equations in two variables
subject: Mathematics
summary: Two linear equations in two variables can be solved graphically or algebraically to find values satisfying both.
points: The graph of each equation is a straight line; the solution is their intersection.
Substitution and elimination are the main algebraic methods.
The pair has one solution, no solution or infinitely many depending on the ratios of coefficients.
example: x + y = 10 and x − y = 2 give x = 6 and y = 4.
mistakes: Forgetting to multiply the constant term as well when scaling an equation.

title: Quadratic equations
subject: Mathematics
summary: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0, and it has at most two roots.
points: The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides the nature of the roots.
D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 gives equal roots, D < 0 gives no real roots.
Roots can be found by factorisation, completing the square or the quadratic formula.
example: x² − 7x + 12 = 0 factors as (x − 3)(x − 4), so x = 3 and x = 4.
mistakes: Using the formula without dividing by 2a.
Dropping the ± sign and reporting only one root.

title: Arithmetic progressions
subject: Mathematics
summary: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term differs from the previous one by a fixed common difference d.
points: The nth term is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
The sum of n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] or n/2 (a + l) where l is the last term.
A sequence is an AP only if the difference between consecutive terms is constant.

formulas.name: nth term
formulas.symbols: a = first term, d = common difference

mistakes: Using n instead of (n − 1) in the nth-term formula.

title: Coordinate geometry
subject: Mathematics
summary: Coordinate geometry places points on a plane using ordered pairs (x, y) and uses formulas to find distances, midpoints and areas.
points: The x-coordinate is the distance from the y-axis; the y-coordinate is the distance from the x-axis.
The distance formula comes from the Pythagoras theorem.
The section formula divides a segment in a given ratio.

formulas.name: Section formula
formulas.expr: ((m x₂ + n x₁)/(m + n), (m y₂ + n y₁)/(m + n))

example: Distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6) is √(9 + 16) = 5.
mistakes: Subtracting coordinates in a different order inside each bracket, which flips signs inconsistently.

title: Triangles: congruence and similarity
subject: Mathematics
summary: Congruent triangles are identical in shape and size; similar triangles have the same shape with proportional sides and equal angles.
points: Congruence tests: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and RHS.
Similarity tests: AA, SSS (proportional sides) and SAS (proportional sides with included angle).
In similar triangles, corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
example: If two triangles have two pairs of equal angles, the third pair is also equal, so they are similar by AA.
mistakes: Assuming AAA proves congruence; it proves similarity only.

title: Trigonometry
subject: Mathematics
summary: Trigonometric ratios relate the angles of a right triangle to the ratios of its sides.
points: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, and tan θ = sin θ / cos θ.
Standard values: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 45° = 1.

formulas.name: Trigonometric ratios
formulas.expr: sin θ = P/H, cos θ = B/H, tan θ = P/B
formulas.symbols: P perpendicular, B base, H hypotenuse

formulas.name: Tangent identity
formulas.expr: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ

example: If the angle of elevation to a tower is 45° and you stand 20 m away, the height is 20 × tan 45° = 20 m.
mistakes: Using the adjacent side where the opposite side is needed.
Forgetting that tan 90° is undefined.

title: Circles and tangents
subject: Mathematics
summary: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point, and its properties connect lengths, angles and chords.
points: The tangent at any point is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
Tangents drawn from an external point are equal in length.
The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
example: If two tangents from P touch a circle at A and B, then PA = PB.
mistakes: Assuming a chord through the centre is a tangent; it is a diameter.

title: Surface areas and volumes
subject: Mathematics
summary: Surface area measures the outside of a solid and volume measures the space inside it.
points: Cylinder: curved surface 2πrh, total 2πr(r + h), volume πr²h.
Cone: curved surface πrl, volume ⅓πr²h, where l = √(r² + h²).
Sphere: surface 4πr², volume 4/3 πr³; hemisphere is half of each.
example: A cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm has volume π × 49 × 10 ≈ 1540 cm³.
mistakes: Using diameter instead of radius.
Forgetting to add the base areas for total surface area.

title: Statistics
subject: Mathematics
summary: Statistics summarises data using measures of central tendency and spread, especially for grouped data.
points: For grouped data, the mean uses class midpoints: x̄ = Σf x / Σf.
The median class is found from cumulative frequency.
The mode is the most frequent value or class.

formulas.name: Median (grouped)
formulas.symbols: l lower limit, cf cumulative frequency before, f frequency, h class size

example: For classes 0–10 (f = 4) and 10–20 (f = 6), the mean uses midpoints 5 and 15: (4×5 + 6×15)/10 = 11.
mistakes: Using class limits instead of midpoints when calculating the mean.

title: Probability
subject: Mathematics
summary: Probability measures the chance of an event and is calculated from equally likely outcomes.
points: 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, with 0 impossible and 1 certain.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
The empirical probability comes from actual trials; theoretical probability comes from counting outcomes.
example: Drawing a king from a standard deck: 4/52 = 1/13.
mistakes: Forgetting to reduce the fraction or exceeding 1.

title: Motion and equations of motion
subject: Physics
summary: For uniformly accelerated motion, three equations connect initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time and displacement.
points: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
The equations apply only when acceleration is constant.
Distance–time and velocity–time graphs describe motion visually.

formulas.name: First equation
formulas.symbols: u initial, v final velocity (m/s), a (m/s²), t (s)

example: A car from rest accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s: v = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s.
mistakes: Using these equations when acceleration is not constant.

title: Newton's laws of motion
subject: Physics
summary: Newton's three laws explain how forces change motion, from inertia to action and reaction.
points: First law: an object stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a net force acts.
Second law: F = ma, so force equals the rate of change of momentum.
Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction on a different body.
example: A 10 kg cart pushed with 20 N accelerates at 2 m/s².
mistakes: Thinking action and reaction cancel because they are equal; they act on different bodies.

title: Gravitation
subject: Physics
summary: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
points: F = G m₁m₂ / r², with G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg².
Weight = mg, and g is about 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface.
Orbital motion is free fall around a planet.
example: Doubling the distance between two masses reduces the gravitational force to one quarter.
mistakes: Saying astronauts in orbit have no gravity; they are in continuous free fall.

title: Work, energy and power
subject: Physics
summary: Work transfers energy, energy is the capacity to do work, and power is the rate of doing work.
points: Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force.
Kinetic energy is ½mv² and potential energy near Earth is mgh.
Power = work ÷ time, measured in watts.

formulas.name: Work
formulas.symbols: θ angle between force and displacement

example: A 60 W bulb left on for 2 hours uses 60 × 7200 = 432,000 J.
mistakes: Ignoring the angle between force and displacement.

title: Sound and waves
subject: Physics
summary: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave, and its frequency, wavelength and speed are linked.
points: Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Audible range for humans is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Echoes are reflected sound; reverberation is repeated reflection in a hall.
example: An echo returns after 0.6 s at 340 m/s, so the reflector is 340 × 0.6 / 2 = 102 m away.
mistakes: Forgetting to halve the distance in echo calculations.

title: Electricity and Ohm's law
subject: Physics
summary: Ohm's law relates potential difference, current and resistance in a conductor at constant temperature.
points: V = IR, with V in volts, I in amperes and R in ohms.
Resistance depends on length, area and material: R = ρl/A.
In series, resistances add; in parallel, the reciprocals add.

formulas.name: Resistivity
formulas.symbols: ρ resistivity, l length, A area

example: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel give 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so R = 3 Ω.
mistakes: Adding parallel resistances directly.

title: Magnetic effects of electric current
subject: Physics
summary: A current-carrying conductor creates a magnetic field, and a conductor in a changing magnetic field can have a current induced in it.
points: The field around a straight wire forms concentric circles; a solenoid produces a uniform field like a bar magnet.
The direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule and Fleming's rules.
Electromagnetic induction is the basis of generators.

formulas.name: Force on a conductor
formulas.expr: F = B I l sin θ
formulas.symbols: B field, I current, l length

example: Moving a magnet into a coil deflects the galvanometer, showing induced current.
mistakes: Thinking a magnet at rest inside a coil induces a steady current; the flux must change.

title: Light: reflection, refraction and lenses
subject: Physics
summary: Light changes direction when it reflects from a surface or refracts as it passes between media of different optical density.
points: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Snell's law: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
A convex lens converges light and a concave lens diverges it.

formulas.name: Snell's law
formulas.expr: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r

example: An object 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm gives 1/v = 1/10 + 1/(−30) = 1/15, so v = 15 cm.
mistakes: Ignoring the sign convention for object distance.

title: The human eye and optical defects
subject: Physics
summary: The eye focuses light on the retina using the cornea and a variable lens, and common defects can be corrected with lenses.
points: The retina detects light and sends signals through the optic nerve.
Myopia (short sight) is corrected with a concave lens; hypermetropia with a convex lens.
Presbyopia is the loss of near focusing with age.
example: A myopic person cannot see distant objects clearly because the image forms in front of the retina.
mistakes: Mixing up which lens corrects myopia; it needs a concave (diverging) lens.

title: Chemical reactions and equations
subject: Chemistry
summary: A chemical equation represents a reaction with formulas, and it must be balanced so atoms are conserved.
points: Types include combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox.
Oxidation is loss of electrons or gain of oxygen; reduction is the reverse.
State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) describe conditions.
example: Rusting is oxidation of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture.
mistakes: Changing subscripts to balance an equation instead of coefficients.

title: Acids, bases and salts
subject: Chemistry
summary: Acids release H⁺ ions in water, bases release OH⁻ ions, and their neutralisation produces salt and water.
points: pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic.
Strong acids and bases ionise completely; weak ones partially.
Common salts include sodium chloride, baking soda and washing soda.
example: A solution with [H⁺] = 10⁻³ mol/L has pH 3 and is acidic.
mistakes: Thinking pH 7 is always neutral in every solvent; it is neutral in water at 25 °C.

title: Metals, non-metals and metallurgy
subject: Chemistry
summary: Metals are extracted from ores by reduction, while non-metals vary widely in properties.
points: Ores are minerals from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
Roasting heats a sulphide ore in air; calcination heats a carbonate ore.
The reactivity series decides the extraction method: electrolysis for reactive metals, reduction for moderate ones.
example: Iron is extracted in a blast furnace by reducing iron oxide with carbon.
mistakes: Thinking all ores are minerals but all minerals are ores; only profitable ones are ores.

title: Carbon and its compounds
subject: Chemistry
summary: Carbon forms covalent bonds with itself and other elements, giving millions of compounds including hydrocarbons and functional groups.
points: Carbon has four valence electrons, so it forms four bonds.
Homologous series differ by CH₂ and share similar chemical properties.
Functional groups such as –OH, –COOH and –CHO determine properties.
example: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) contains the alcohol group; ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) contains the carboxyl group.
mistakes: Writing the alkene formula as CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

title: Periodic classification
subject: Chemistry
summary: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, so elements with similar properties fall in the same group.
points: Groups are vertical columns and periods are horizontal rows.
Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.
example: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all group 1 alkali metals and react similarly with water.
mistakes: Thinking atomic size increases across a period; it decreases as nuclear charge grows.

title: Chemical bonding
subject: Chemistry
summary: Atoms bond to gain a stable electron arrangement, forming ionic bonds by transfer and covalent bonds by sharing.
points: Ionic compounds form between metals and non-metals and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.
Covalent compounds form between non-metals and usually have low melting points.
Metallic bonding explains conductivity and malleability.
example: NaCl is ionic: sodium loses an electron and chlorine gains it.
mistakes: Saying ionic compounds conduct as solids; the ions must be free to move.

title: Mole concept
subject: Chemistry
summary: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles and equals the molar mass in grams of a substance.
points: n = given mass ÷ molar mass.
One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.
Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole.

formulas.name: Moles
formulas.symbols: m mass in g, M molar mass in g/mol

example: 18 g of water is 1 mol, containing 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.
mistakes: Using mass in kg in n = m/M.

title: Life processes: nutrition
subject: Biology
summary: Nutrition provides organisms with energy and materials, through photosynthesis in plants and digestion in animals.
points: Autotrophic nutrition makes food from simple substances; heterotrophic nutrition depends on others.
Human digestion uses mechanical and chemical breakdown with enzymes.
Balanced nutrition needs carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
example: Amoeba engulfs food by pseudopodia, a form of holozoic nutrition.
mistakes: Thinking digestion is only mechanical; enzymes do the chemical work.

title: Respiration and transport
subject: Biology
summary: Respiration releases energy from food, and transport systems carry oxygen, nutrients and waste around the body.
points: Human respiration uses lungs with alveoli for gas exchange.
The heart has four chambers; arteries, veins and capillaries form the circulation.
Plants transport water through xylem and food through phloem.
example: Alveoli have thin walls and a large surface area for efficient gas exchange.
mistakes: Saying arteries always carry oxygenated blood; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

title: Excretion
subject: Biology
summary: Excretion removes metabolic waste, and the kidneys filter blood to produce urine.
points: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
Filtration, reabsorption and secretion produce urine.
Plants excrete waste through leaves, bark and roots.
example: Useful glucose and most water are reabsorbed in the kidney tubule, so urine is concentrated.
mistakes: Confusing excretion (removing metabolic waste) with egestion (removing undigested food).

title: Control and coordination
subject: Biology
summary: The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate body responses, using electrical impulses and hormones.
points: A neuron carries impulses; synapses pass them to the next cell.
The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system.
Hormones such as insulin and adrenaline act more slowly than nerves.
example: Adrenaline raises heart rate and prepares the body for a quick response.
mistakes: Thinking reflex actions are decided by the brain; the spinal cord handles many of them.

title: Reproduction
subject: Biology
summary: Reproduction produces new individuals, asexually in many organisms and sexually through specialised gametes.
points: Asexual methods include binary fission, budding and regeneration.
In humans, fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube and the embryo develops in the uterus.
Flowers are the reproductive organs of angiosperms.
example: Hydra reproduces by budding, while humans reproduce sexually.
mistakes: Saying fertilisation happens in the uterus; it normally happens in the fallopian tube.

title: Heredity and evolution
subject: Biology
summary: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring through genes, and evolution is change in populations over generations.
points: Genes are segments of DNA; alleles are alternative forms of a gene.
Mendel's laws explain dominant and recessive inheritance.
Natural selection favours traits that improve survival and reproduction.
example: Crossing a pure tall pea plant with a pure short one gives tall offspring in the first generation.
mistakes: Thinking a dominant allele is more common; dominance is about expression, not frequency.

title: Environment and ecosystems
subject: Biology
summary: Organisms depend on their environment, and human activity can damage the ecosystems that support them.
points: Food chains and webs show energy flow; only about 10% passes to the next level.
Pollution, deforestation and waste reduce biodiversity.
Conservation and sustainable use protect ecosystems.
example: Ozone depletion is caused mainly by chlorofluorocarbons and increases harmful UV radiation.
mistakes: Thinking the 10% energy rule means energy is destroyed; it is lost mainly as heat.

title: The French Revolution
subject: History
summary: The French Revolution (1789) overthrew the absolute monarchy and feudal privileges in France and spread ideas of liberty, equality and fraternity.
points: Causes included financial crisis, heavy taxation of the Third Estate and Enlightenment ideas.
The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 became its symbol.
It led to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and eventually to Napoleon's rise.
example: The Third Estate paid most taxes but had little political power, which fuelled resentment.
mistakes: Saying the revolution ended the monarchy immediately; France became a republic in 1792.

title: The Russian Revolution
subject: History
summary: The Russian Revolution of 1917 ended tsarist rule and brought the Bolsheviks to power under Lenin.
points: The February Revolution overthrew Tsar Nicholas II; the October Revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power.
Causes included war hardship, food shortages and inequality.
It created the Soviet Union and influenced socialist movements worldwide.
example: The slogan 'peace, land and bread' addressed the main grievances of soldiers, peasants and workers.
aliases: socialism in europe and the russian revolution
mistakes: Treating the February and October revolutions as a single event.

title: Nationalism in Europe
subject: History
summary: In nineteenth-century Europe, nationalism united some states and divided others, reshaping the map by 1914.
points: The French Revolution spread ideas of the nation as a community of citizens.
Italy and Germany were unified in the nineteenth century.
Nationalism also produced aggressive imperialism and Balkan tensions.
example: Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers helped unify Italy, while Bismarck unified Germany through war and diplomacy.
mistakes: Assuming nationalism was only a force for liberation; it also drove expansion and conflict.

title: Nationalism in India
subject: History
summary: Indian nationalism grew into a mass movement against colonial rule, using non-violent protest, boycotts and civil disobedience.
points: The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh massacre deepened anger at British rule.
Gandhi linked swaraj to khadi, village industry and Hindu–Muslim unity.
The Salt March of 1930 began the Civil Disobedience Movement.
example: The Simon Commission was boycotted because it had no Indian members.
mistakes: Describing the movement as only Gandhi's work; peasants, workers and women shaped it too.

title: Nazism and the rise of Hitler
subject: History
summary: Nazism was the fascist ideology of the German Nazi Party, which ruled Germany under Adolf Hitler from 1933 and carried out the Holocaust.
points: The Great Depression and humiliation after the First World War weakened the Weimar Republic.
Nazi ideology promoted racial hierarchy, antisemitism and expansion.
The regime murdered six million Jews and millions of others in the Holocaust.
example: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped Jewish Germans of citizenship rights.
aliases: nazism and the rise of hitler
mistakes: Treating Nazism as only a German problem; it drew on wider racist and imperial ideas.

title: India: location and size
subject: Geography
summary: India lies in South Asia between latitudes 8°4′N and 37°6′N and longitudes 68°7′E and 97°25′E.
points: The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of the country.
India has a long coastline and the Himalayas as a natural northern boundary.
The Indian Standard Meridian is 82°30′E.
example: India's east–west extent creates a time difference of about two hours between Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat.
mistakes: Forgetting that the Tropic of Cancer divides India into almost two equal parts.

title: Physical features of India
subject: Geography
summary: India has six major physical divisions: the Himalayas, northern plains, peninsular plateau, coastal plains, islands and the Indian desert.
points: The Himalayas are young fold mountains with three ranges: Himadri, Himachal and Shivaliks.
The northern plains are formed by alluvium from the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.
The peninsular plateau is old, stable and rich in minerals.
example: The Deccan Plateau is part of the peninsular plateau and is made of old volcanic rock.
mistakes: Treating the Himalayas and the peninsular plateau as the same age; the plateau is much older.

title: Drainage systems of India
subject: Geography
summary: India's rivers are grouped into Himalayan rivers, which are perennial, and peninsular rivers, which depend on rainfall.
points: The Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra rise beyond the Himalayas and flow all year.
Peninsular rivers such as the Godavari and Krishna are seasonal.
River basins supply water for irrigation, industry and cities.
example: The Ganga basin is India's largest river basin and supports dense agriculture.
mistakes: Assuming all Indian rivers flow east; the Narmada and Tapi flow west.

title: Minerals and energy resources
subject: Geography
summary: Minerals and energy resources power industry, but most are non-renewable and need careful use.
points: Minerals occur in veins, beds, alluvial deposits and as rocks.
Conventional energy includes coal, petroleum and natural gas; non-conventional includes solar, wind and biogas.
Recycling and efficient use extend limited resources.
example: Coal is used mainly for electricity generation and is a major source of carbon emissions.
mistakes: Calling coal renewable because it forms from plants; it takes millions of years.

title: Manufacturing industries
subject: Geography
summary: Manufacturing turns raw materials into finished goods and is located where transport, labour, power and markets are favourable.
points: Agro-based industries use farm products; mineral-based industries use minerals.
Iron and steel is a basic industry because others depend on it.
Industries cause pollution and need cleaner technology.
example: Cotton textile mills cluster near cotton-growing areas and ports.
mistakes: Thinking industry location depends on one factor; several costs interact.

title: Power sharing and federalism
subject: Political Science
summary: Power sharing distributes authority among institutions and levels of government, and federalism divides power between the centre and states.
points: Belgium and Sri Lanka show different approaches to ethnic power sharing.
India is a federal state with a strong centre, three lists and residuary powers.
Decentralisation to local bodies deepens participation.
example: India's Union List, State List and Concurrent List divide legislative subjects.
mistakes: Calling India a pure confederation; the centre has significant powers.

title: Electoral politics
subject: Political Science
summary: Elections are the mechanism through which citizens choose representatives, and their credibility depends on fairness and participation.
points: The Election Commission conducts elections and enforces the model code of conduct.
Universal adult franchise gives every citizen aged 18 and above the vote.
Free and fair elections require an updated roll, secret ballot and fair campaign rules.
example: An electronic voting machine records a vote in secret and reduces counting errors.
mistakes: Thinking elections alone make a democracy; rights, rule of law and accountability matter too.

title: Political parties
subject: Political Science
summary: Political parties organise people around programmes, contest elections and form or oppose governments.
points: A party needs policies, members and a leadership structure.
India has national, state and regional parties.
Parties face challenges such as dynastic control and money power.
example: A coalition government forms when no single party wins a majority.
mistakes: Assuming parties are only election machines; they also shape policy and public debate.

title: Outcomes of democracy
subject: Political Science
summary: Democracy is judged by accountability, responsiveness, equality and the protection of rights, not only by economic growth.
points: Democratic governments are accountable to citizens and can be voted out.
Democracy handles diversity and social conflict through negotiation.
It can be slow and may fail to reduce inequality without active participation.
example: Transparency and the right to information let citizens question official decisions.
mistakes: Judging democracy only by economic performance; political and social outcomes matter too.

title: Gender, religion and caste
subject: Political Science
summary: Gender, religion and caste shape politics in India, and the Constitution tries to ensure equality while allowing diversity.
points: Patriarchy limits women's public participation; reservations aim to correct this.
Communalism treats one religion as superior and threatens secularism.
Caste politics can mobilise excluded groups but also entrench divisions.
example: One-third reservation for women in local bodies increased their political representation.
mistakes: Confusing secularism with anti-religion; Indian secularism treats all religions equally.

title: Development
subject: Economics
summary: Development means improvement in people's lives, measured by income as well as health, education and freedom.
points: Per capita income is average income, which hides inequality.
The Human Development Index combines income, education and health.
Different people and regions may want different things from development.
example: Two countries with the same average income can have very different literacy and health outcomes.
mistakes: Treating higher average income as the only sign of development.

title: Sectors of the Indian economy
subject: Economics
summary: Economic activity is grouped into primary (extraction), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services) sectors.
points: Primary includes farming, mining and fishing.
Secondary turns raw materials into goods.
Tertiary provides services such as transport, banking and education.
example: Turning cotton into cloth is secondary activity; selling the cloth is tertiary.
mistakes: Placing transport in the secondary sector; it is a service.

title: Money and banking
subject: Economics
summary: Money is a medium of exchange, and banks accept deposits, lend and create credit.
points: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants in barter.
The Reserve Bank of India issues currency and regulates banks.
Banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest.
example: With a 10% reserve ratio, ₹1,000 of new deposits can support up to ₹10,000 of deposits.
mistakes: Thinking banks keep all deposits available for withdrawal at once.

title: Globalisation
subject: Economics
summary: Globalisation is the growing integration of economies through trade, investment, technology and migration.
points: Multinational companies invest across borders and link production chains.
Trade barriers such as tariffs reduce integration; liberalisation removes them.
Globalisation can create jobs and cheaper goods but also insecurity for workers.
example: A phone designed in one country, with parts from several and assembled in another, shows a global value chain.
mistakes: Assuming globalisation benefits everyone equally; gains and losses are uneven.

title: Consumer rights
subject: Economics
summary: Consumer rights protect buyers from unfair trade practices, unsafe goods and misleading information.
points: Rights include safety, information, choice, being heard and redressal.
A consumer court can order compensation for defective goods.
The Consumer Protection Act and standardisation marks help enforce quality.
example: A shop cannot refuse a bill for a product it sells; the bill is proof for a complaint.
mistakes: Thinking consumer rights apply only to expensive purchases.

title: Poverty and employment
subject: Economics
summary: Poverty is the inability to meet basic needs, and employment patterns decide whether work lifts people out of it.
points: Poverty is measured using income or consumption lines and multidimensional indicators.
Informal and disguised unemployment are widespread in Indian agriculture.
Education, health and social protection reduce poverty.
example: Five family members farming a small plot may all be working, but some are in disguised unemployment.
mistakes: Confusing unemployment with low wages; people can be working and still poor.
